clinicalPearls: Combines profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss with a markedly prolonged QT interval on the ECG
Caused by biallelic mutations in KCNQ1 (or less often KCNE1), which encode subunits of a potassium channel; inheritance is autosomal recessive
The same channel is needed for endolymph production in the inner ear and for cardiac repolarisation, explaining the combined phenotype
Presents with syncope, seizures or sudden collapse triggered by exertion, emotion or startle, reflecting torsades de pointes
Any deaf child with unexplained syncope, seizures or a family history of sudden death must have an ECG to look for QT prolongation
Heterozygous carriers may have isolated long QT (Romano-Ward pattern) without deafness
Cardiac risk is high and untreated patients face a substantial risk of sudden cardiac death, so cardiology referral is urgent
reference.pathophysiology: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNQ1 or KCNE1, subunits forming the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current channel. In the stria vascularis of the inner ear this current is essential for secreting potassium-rich endolymph; its loss disrupts the endocochlear potential and causes profound congenital sensorineural deafness. In cardiac myocytes the same current contributes to repolarisation, so its loss prolongs the action potential and the QT interval, predisposing to torsades de pointes ventricular arrhythmia, syncope and sudden death. The recessive combined phenotype requires two defective alleles, whereas single-allele defects tend to cause isolated long QT syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Romano-Ward long QT syndrome without deafness
Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance
Seizure disorder or epilepsy misattributed to a primary neurological cause
Other syndromic congenital sensorineural hearing loss
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and other inherited arrhythmias
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead ECG with corrected QT measurement, the key diagnostic test
Audiometry including auditory brainstem response to confirm profound hearing loss
Ambulatory ECG and exercise testing to capture arrhythmia and QT behaviour
Serum electrolytes to exclude reversible causes of QT prolongation
Molecular genetic testing of KCNQ1 and KCNE1 and cascade screening of relatives
redFlags: Syncope, seizures or cardiac arrest, particularly during exertion, emotion or sudden noise
Family history of sudden unexplained death or long QT syndrome
Documented torsades de pointes or very prolonged corrected QT interval
Exposure to QT-prolonging medications that could precipitate arrhythmia
reference.prognosis: Untreated the syndrome carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from malignant arrhythmia, but prognosis improves substantially with beta-blockade, avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs, and consideration of an implantable defibrillator, alongside hearing rehabilitation for the profound deafness.
pitfalls: Not performing an ECG in a deaf child with syncope or seizures and missing the cardiac diagnosis
Misdiagnosing arrhythmic collapse as epilepsy and delaying cardiac treatment
Prescribing QT-prolonging medications, which can precipitate fatal arrhythmia
Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to screen at-risk relatives
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Start lifelong non-selective beta-blockade (nadolol or propranolol) as first-line protection against catecholamine-driven torsades de pointes
Avoid all QT-prolonging drugs and counsel on agents to be shunned lifelong
Correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and iron-deficiency anaemia to remove reversible arrhythmic triggers
Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator after aborted cardiac arrest or for arrhythmia recurring despite beta-blockade
Consider left cardiac sympathetic denervation when events persist on maximal drug therapy
Provide cochlear implantation and hearing rehabilitation for the profound bilateral sensorineural deafness
Arrange autosomal recessive genetic counselling with cascade ECG and genetic screening of relatives
Restrict startle and strenuous exertion triggers and seek urgent cardiology review for syncope or documented arrhythmia
